paper.title: Self-supervised Contrastive Learning for EEG-based Sleep Staging

thesis: Contrastive pretraining on transformed unlabeled EEG improves sleep-stage classification, especially when labels are scarce, but does not remove the persistent difficulty of N1 staging.

nodes.title: Can unlabeled EEG improve sleep staging?
nodes.body: Test whether contrastive self-supervision learns representations that reduce dependence on costly expert sleep-stage labels.

nodes.title: Contrast transformed views
nodes.body: Construct positive pairs from signal transformations and train an encoder before supervised fine-tuning.

nodes.title: Pretrain on Sleep-EDF EEG
nodes.body: Use 100 Hz Fpz–Cz recordings from twenty healthy adults and evaluate five-stage classification.

nodes.title: Compare transformation pairs
nodes.body: Ablate combinations of permutation, crop-and-resize and other EEG transformations.

nodes.title: Permutation plus crop wins
nodes.body: Permutation with crop-and-resize produced the strongest transformation-pair result.

nodes.title: Full-label accuracy improves
nodes.body: Self-supervised pretraining raises accuracy from 86.60% to 88.16% and macro F1 from 79.51% to 81.96%.

nodes.title: Benefit grows under label scarcity
nodes.body: With ten labeled examples per class, SSL reaches 67.826% accuracy versus 49.176% for random initialization.

nodes.title: Self-supervision reduces label dependence
nodes.body: Unlabeled EEG supplies useful representations for downstream sleep staging across full- and limited-label settings.

nodes.title: N1 remains difficult
nodes.body: The minority N1 stage remains a major source of confusion despite improved aggregate metrics.

openQuestions: The fixture does not contain subject-level predictions, so demographic and per-subject error patterns cannot be inspected in the prototype.
